# Mico canvas evaluation

Run this workflow from the Mico repository root as the coordinator. The cases in `evals/` are frozen inputs: each `prompt.md` is given to the drawing agent; `rubric.md` is for the coordinator only. Compare the same prompts, model, tools, viewport and scoring rules across revisions. Record any deviation rather than implying a controlled comparison.

## Safety and isolation

- Never use the daily board (`.mico/board.sqlite`, ports 7063/37063) for an evaluation. Do not copy it, clear it or seed it.
- Run one isolated case at a time in the existing Herdr `dev server` tab. Create a fresh private directory with `mktemp -d /tmp/mico-eval-XXXXXX`, choose a fresh UUID as the run identity, then run `pnpm eval:server /tmp/<directory>/board.sqlite <identity>` in a foreground shell there. Confirm the identity and empty board at `http://127.0.0.1:27063/__eval_identity` and `http://127.0.0.1:57063/api/board`. If either port is in use, stop rather than targeting an unknown service.
- Evaluation captures use the isolated loopback URL, not the daily Caddy origin. Never modify shared Caddy, certificates, or other users' processes as part of this workflow.
- Set `MICO_PORT=57063` in the drawing pane. Tell the agent to use only the isolated board, not read `evals/`, not edit the repository, and put temporary scripts in `/tmp`. Give it the exact text of `prompt.md`, without the rubric, answers or layout instructions. Let it independently discover and use the public Mico interface. It may inspect and refine its own work.
- Create a **new interactive coding pane and fresh agent session for every case and every round**. Use the same model and thinking settings each time. Follow the local Herdr rules; close each owned pane after retrieving evidence. Never reuse a drawing session between cases or rounds.

## Run and inspect

1. Record the source revision, case prompt, model/provider, start time, pane/session identity, isolated endpoint and any additional coordinator messages. Start with an empty isolated board.
2. Wait for the agent to finish. Preserve its tool calls, errors, responses and final message as a transcript without image payloads or private reasoning; do not report an infrastructure failure as a drawing result.
3. Create `evals/<case>/runs/<UTC timestamp>-<round>/`. Run `pnpm eval:capture <run-directory> <identity>` with the identity chosen before starting the fixture. This saves `board.json` and a 1440×960 Chrome `screenshot.png`; failure is explicit and should still retain whatever evidence can be captured. Keep the run even when empty or failed. Check that the captured revision and screenshot match and that the browser shows a live connection.
4. Open the screenshot and assess each criterion in `rubric.md`, factual accuracy, visual readability and whether the requested visual information is actually visible. Save a short `assessment.md` with points and concrete evidence. A valid API response is not proof of a good drawing. Note agent friction, rejected operations, rendering defects and whether a failure is in the task, model, API, or renderer; do not infer root cause without evidence.
5. Save metadata and checksums, terminate only the owned fixture in its Herdr pane, remove only its temporary database and cache, and close the drawing pane. Repeat with a fresh fixture and pane for the next case.

## Compare and repair

Complete all 10 baseline cases before changing the canvas implementation. Group reproducible problems, add regression tests, fix root causes with minimal changes and independent review, then rerun the same 10 cases on the repaired revision with fresh panes and boards. Compare paired scores and screenshots per case; discuss model variability and avoid attributing every difference to the code change. Keep failures and non-comparable runs in the report. Commit logical changes and evidence atomically on `main`; never overwrite earlier runs.

README.md:3:A local-first canvas experiment where people and local agents edit the same board. The browser renders the canvas; the daemon owns the board and stores it in SQLite; the CLI gives agents direct access to the same operations.
README.md:23:Open <https://mico.dev.hexly.ai/>. Caddy proxies to Vite on `127.0.0.1:7063`; Vite proxies `/api` (including WebSocket upgrades) to the loopback-only daemon on `127.0.0.1:37063`. The browser uses same-origin HTTPS/WSS, never mixed-content loopback requests. The daemon stores its board in `.mico/board.sqlite`.
README.md:25:Vite hot-reloads frontend changes; `pnpm daemon` watches daemon source changes and restarts automatically. API and CLI writes update open canvases live over WebSocket, with automatic reconnection and a three-second polling fallback. `MICO_PORT` overrides the daemon port for the daemon, CLI, and Vite proxy; set it consistently in both terminals. `MICO_DB_PATH` overrides the database path.
README.md:27:Port allocation: development `7063`, E2E `17063`, browser/BDD `27063`, internal daemon `37063`. Automated tests must use an isolated database and loopback endpoint, not the daily board. The shared Caddy mapping lives in `workflow/caddy/Caddyfile` and the active machine's `/opt/homebrew/etc/Caddyfile`; the existing `*.dev.hexly.ai` certificate covers this hostname.
README.md:29:The canvas supports panning, zooming, rectangles, ellipses, typographic text, lines, freehand brush strokes, sticky notes, frames, rich widgets, connectors, dragging, snapping, marquee selection, color and deletion. Boards fit the viewport on first load; click Fit or press F to fit all objects again.
README.md:31:Drag on empty canvas with Select to marquee several objects, then Delete removes them atomically. Frame selection wraps the current selection in a named card with 32px padding; dragging the frame moves its members, and deleting the frame releases them without deleting content. Sticky notes (N) use a five-colour palette and multi-line text. Text (T) has no box; choose Hand, Serif, Sans or Mono with 16/24/32/48px sizes and 300/400/500/700 weights for editorial layouts.
README.md:33:The Rich widget tool (W) creates an isolated card: checklist, kanban, table or timeline. Its title and items are editable in the bottom dock, and other objects cannot be dropped or created inside it; overlays remain possible. Agents can create widgets, frames, notes and typographic text through the same batch API.
README.md:35:Select the Brush tool (P) and drag to draw. The dock exposes three brush styles — pencil, marker and tapered brush — and 2/4/8px widths. Strokes persist as `path` shapes, so selecting one lets you change its brush, width and color. AI agents create the same shapes through the batch API; `examples/sketch.ts` draws a house, stick figure, sun and hills with 23 tapered strokes. Select the hand tool or hold Space and drag to pan. For connectors, select the connector tool and drag from a source node toward a target. Nearby nodes reveal their anchors; the highlighted anchor is the exact persisted attachment. Select a connector to drag either endpoint to another node. Dropping on empty space, cancelling a pointer, or pressing Escape leaves it unchanged. Source and Target controls in the dock properties provide a keyboard alternative. Concurrent agent edits are checked before committing a drag.
README.md:39:The canvas uses a subtle blueprint grid: a solid line every 64px with four dashed 16px cells between solid lines at 100% zoom. Reference sampling of the Miro screenshot measured a 242 base gray with 238 grid lines; Mico keeps that near-neutral calm while retaining a slightly stronger major line for hierarchy. The grid follows world pan and zoom; dashed detail fades at low zoom to avoid moiré.
README.md:41:The identity panel shows only the logo and a breathing connection light, and the unified bottom dock is fixed in screen space: canvas pan and zoom never resize, move or hide them. Drawing tools, zoom/reset, Fit and the selected object's properties share one dock; narrow viewports wrap its controls instead of clipping them. The color panel opens above the dock. Controls use fixed 40px height, 20px icons and 14px text on a four-pixel spacing system: dock padding, gaps, dividers, property columns and selection insets are all multiples of four. The dock sizes to its content, grows when an object is selected, and keeps a four-pixel gap between buttons. Lucide icons keep hover-only shortcut hints. Toolbar arrow keys move focus; Enter selects a tool.

README.md:61:A canvas shape has `id`, `type` (`rectangle`, `ellipse`, `text`, or `line`), `x`, `y`, `w`, `h`, `color` (six-digit hex for stroke or line color), and optional `text`. Rectangles and ellipses may also set `fill` to a six-digit hex color or `null`; `null` is transparent, while omitting `fill` preserves the existing surface fill. `fill` is not valid on text, lines, paths, frames, notes, widgets or connectors. Text, rectangle and ellipse labels accept optional `font` (`sans`, `serif`, `hand`, `mono`), `fontSize` (8–256) and `fontWeight` (100–900). Rectangle and ellipse labels preserve newlines and wrap within the label area; text that cannot fit remains visible with an overflow marker rather than being silently truncated. For a line, `w` and `h` are signed offsets to its endpoint and optional `strokeWidth` (1–64) controls the visible stroke. A connector has `id`, `type: "connector"`, `from` and `to` shape IDs, and `color`. A `path` shape has `points` (2–4096 points relative to its `x`/`y`, inside its `w`/`h` bounds), `brush` (`pencil`, `marker`, `brush`) and `strokeWidth` (1–64). Paths use the same anchors, dragging and snapping as other shapes. Validation rejects out-of-bounds points or unknown brushes atomically with the rest of the batch. Optional `fromAnchor` and `toAnchor` pin either endpoint to an exact anchor index: boxes/text/ellipses have 12 anchors, lines have five. Pins must be non-negative integers inside the referenced node's anchor range; invalid pins reject the entire batch. Unpinned endpoints use automatic nearest-outward routing. Pinned attachments follow their nodes as they move.


The distributed-commerce example adds 20 services and clients, 27 connectors, and six headings to the right of the original Mico diagram without deleting existing objects. Its fixed `commerce-` IDs make duplicate application fail atomically. Click Fit after adding it to an open board.

`shape create` generates an ID if one is omitted. A batch is an array of `create`, `update`, or `delete` operations; use `-` instead of a filename to read JSON from standard input. Batch-created shapes must include IDs so that connectors can refer to them. The example uses fixed IDs and can be applied once to an empty board. Deleting a shape also deletes connectors attached to it; connector endpoints must be different.

A canvas shape has `id`, `type` (`rectangle`, `ellipse`, `text`, or `line`), `x`, `y`, `w`, `h`, `color` (six-digit hex for stroke or line color), and optional `text`. Rectangles and ellipses may also set `fill` to a six-digit hex color or `null`; `null` is transparent, while omitting `fill` preserves the existing surface fill. `fill` is not valid on text, lines, paths, frames, notes, widgets or connectors. Text, rectangle and ellipse labels accept optional `font` (`sans`, `serif`, `hand`, `mono`), `fontSize` (8–256) and `fontWeight` (100–900). Rectangle and ellipse labels preserve newlines and wrap within the label area; text that cannot fit remains visible with an overflow marker rather than being silently truncated. For a line, `w` and `h` are signed offsets to its endpoint and optional `strokeWidth` (1–64) controls the visible stroke. A connector has `id`, `type: "connector"`, `from` and `to` shape IDs, and `color`. A `path` shape has `points` (2–4096 points relative to its `x`/`y`, inside its `w`/`h` bounds), `brush` (`pencil`, `marker`, `brush`) and `strokeWidth` (1–64). Paths use the same anchors, dragging and snapping as other shapes. Validation rejects out-of-bounds points or unknown brushes atomically with the rest of the batch. Optional `fromAnchor` and `toAnchor` pin either endpoint to an exact anchor index: boxes/text/ellipses have 12 anchors, lines have five. Pins must be non-negative integers inside the referenced node's anchor range; invalid pins reject the entire batch. Unpinned endpoints use automatic nearest-outward routing. Pinned attachments follow their nodes as they move.

Browser page zoom is disabled with a viewport lock plus keyboard/gesture interception; canvas zoom remains separate. The daemon exposes `GET /api/live` (status and manifest-derived version), `GET /api/board`, `POST /api/operations`, and a WebSocket at `/api/events`. A batch is validated and persisted atomically. An optional `expectedRevision` rejects writes based on stale board state. WebSocket subscribers receive the complete current board on connection and after each mutation.

## Verification

```sh
pnpm check
pnpm test
pnpm build
pnpm test:browser
```

Browser checks require installed Google Chrome and run sequentially on `127.0.0.1:27063`, with an isolated daemon on `57063`, a temporary SQLite database, and a separate Vite cache. The suite refuses to seed another origin and never changes the daily `.mico` board. It covers frame alignment, icon/tooltip behavior, dock property editing, drag snapping with alignment guides, connector creation/rebinding/cancellation, keyboard alternatives, concurrent API edits, grid/world alignment and unchanged frame geometry from 5% to 300% zoom. Responsive checks keep every dock control and its color panel visible at narrow and wide widths.

## MVP limits

This is a single local board, not a multi-user server. It has no authentication beyond restricting browser origins and hosts, and trusts processes running on the local machine. Do not expose the daemon to a network. Undo/redo, resizing, remote deployment, and MCP are not implemented yet.

interface Stroke {
	id: string
	color: string
	brush: 'pencil' | 'marker' | 'brush'
	strokeWidth: number
	points: { x: number; y: number }[]
}

const strokes: Stroke[] = []
const ink = '#242424'
const base = { x: 1760, y: 980 }

function curve(
	id: string,
	points: [number, number][],
	options: Partial<Pick<Stroke, 'brush' | 'strokeWidth' | 'color'>> = {},
) {
	strokes.push({
		id,
		color: options.color ?? ink,
		brush: options.brush ?? 'brush',
		strokeWidth: options.strokeWidth ?? 4,
		points: points.map(([x, y]) => ({ x: base.x + x, y: base.y + y })),
	})
}

function arc(
	id: string,
	cx: number,
	cy: number,
	radiusX: number,
	radiusY: number,
	from: number,
	to: number,
	steps = 24,
	options: Partial<Pick<Stroke, 'brush' | 'strokeWidth' | 'color'>> = {},
) {
	curve(
		id,
		Array.from({ length: steps + 1 }, (_, index) => {
			const angle = from + ((to - from) * index) / steps
			return [cx + Math.cos(angle) * radiusX, cy + Math.sin(angle) * radiusY] as [number, number]
		}),
		options,
	)
}
